commitHorizon.explanation: Inversions fall as the horizon grows, because the horizon has to cover how long a join takes to commit rather than how far apart arrivals are. The cost is that every customer waits at least the horizon longer, so the right setting is the smallest one that holds under the commit latency the service actually sees under load — which is why this is measured rather than picked.

environment.notes: WSL2 on Windows, 8 cores, 8 GB RAM. Postgres 16.15 and Redis on the same host, fsync on, synchronous_commit on. 1 allocator node(s); simulator capped at 1500 concurrent connections. Simulated customers are not simultaneous sockets: offered arrival rate, peak concurrent connections and completed purchases are reported separately.

fairness.profileNote: A lottery is only as unfair as the arrival process lets it be. Drawing at             random from everyone waiting looks close to FIFO when customers trickle in,             because the pool to draw from only contains people who have already arrived.             The policies separate under a thundering herd, where everyone is waiting at             once and the draw is over the whole population — which is why both profiles             are reported rather than whichever one flatters the result.

shardSweep.nextBottleneckEvidence: At the plateau the shard rows are no longer the limit. Peak concurrent connections reached 1500 against the simulator's cap, and checkout p99 at the highest shard count was 2192.4 ms, so the remaining cost is per-request work — connection handling, the Postgres round-trip per probe, and the simulator's own concurrency ceiling — rather than contention on a single row.

sweepStrategy.note: Reservations are reclaimed in bounded batches, one transaction each, so a             large backlog cannot hold locks proportional to its size or stall allocation             while it drains. The node sweeps continuously as well, so the figure that             matters is the time for the pool to come back in full rather than how many             any one sweeper happened to claim. Measured on node             node-0 with the strategy it was started with; set             SWEEP_STRATEGY=indexScan or bucketed and re-run to compare the two, since             two sweepers in one process would contend for the same rows.

tailFragmentation.summary: Last 5% of inventory over 64 shards, pooled over 8 trials per arm, with             fewer requests in each wave than units remaining so every failure is             fragmentation rather than a sell-out. Without collapse: 60 of 159 requests             failed while stock remained (37.7%), with stock sitting on about 18 of 64             shards. With collapse: 52 of 164 (31.7%).
